caption:
Paul Christiano, who joined OpenAI's board in September, told a Toronto audience that an AI accident is the most likely way most of them will die.
He puts the chance of humans losing control of AI at 4% within a year and 15% within three.
He also says the industry, OpenAI included, is not on track to lower that risk.

Is he right, or is this too much?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

paragraphs.text: Paul Christiano, a member of the OpenAI Foundation board, told an audience at the 2026 Hinton Lectures in Toronto that an AI accident is the most likely way most of them will die, according to reports by Newsweek, Gizmodo and Fast Company published between November 11 and November 13, 2026.

Christiano joined the board in September to help oversee the company's safety practices, Gizmodo reported. He also sits on its Safety and Security Committee and is the founder of the Alignment Research Center.

"For most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident," Christiano said, as quoted by all three outlets. Newsweek reported that he also called the trajectory of the field "extremely alarming over the last three to six months."

According to Newsweek, he said the industry had seen "roughly the things we might expect to see shortly before something really bad would happen," and described advanced AI as a second species that vastly outnumbers and outsmarts humans.

Fast Company reported that Christiano described an AI takeover as a situation in which AI systems pursue goals of their own, and said that human attempts to resist one would be as ineffective as an individual trying to stop the U.S. military.

In September, when he joined the board, Christiano estimated a 4 percent chance that humans lose control of AI within one year and a 15 percent chance within three years. He has described those figures as subjective judgments, both Gizmodo and Fast Company noted.

If labs build as fast as they can without outside intervention, he put the odds of an AI takeover within three years at roughly a coin flip. Fast Company quoted him saying that even with realistic policy responses, the risk remains exceptionally high.

The outlets describe his timeline in different terms. Gizmodo wrote that he sees a meaningful risk of an AI takeover in the next 6 to 12 months, while Newsweek reported a warning about possible takeover attempts within the next three years.

In a personal statement published when he joined OpenAI's board, Christiano wrote that the AI industry in general, including OpenAI, is not currently on track to reduce this risk, according to Newsweek. Fast Company cited the same statement, in which he warned that building superintelligence without more robust alignment would likely mean permanently losing control of it.

Gizmodo also cited other researchers who give short timelines. Eli Lifland of the AI Futures Project pointed to a window of 3 to 12 months, and Buck Shlegeris of Redwood Research put the chance that misaligned AI disrupts normal life within a year at about 20 percent.

Christiano did not argue that the outcome is fixed. Fast Company reported that he credits AI companies with the ability to avoid the coin flip scenario by "pacing the frontier," a phrase that echoes an essay by Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei. Newsweek's report did not include a response from OpenAI.

The warning stands out because of where it comes from. Christiano is not an outside critic. He sits on the board that oversees OpenAI's safety work, and he is saying in public that the industry, including the company he helps govern, is not doing enough to lower the risk. His probabilities are personal estimates rather than measurements, and he labels them that way, but they come from a person with direct oversight of one of the largest AI developers.

The next thing to watch is whether OpenAI or its Safety and Security Committee responds publicly, and whether the slower, paced approach Christiano describes shows up in how OpenAI releases its next models.
